final_proof:
There are two type errors in the explanatory bullets of the statement. Since L: D → C, the opposite functor has type L^op: D^op → C^op, not C^op → D^op. Also, the ordinary hom bifunctor of C has type Hom_C(−,−): C^op × C → Set, not D^op × C → Set. Thus, if the erroneous types are read literally, the claimed composite is not defined. With these necessary corrections, the displayed equality is well-typed and true.

Because C is locally small, every Hom_C(Y,X) is a set, so the ordinary hom bifunctor to Set is defined. The product functor

L^op × id_C: D^op × C → C^op × C

sends an object (A,X) to (LA,X). Therefore, for every A in D and X in C,

(Hom_C(−,−) ∘ (L^op × id_C))(A,X) = Hom_C(LA,X).

This is exactly the object assignment of Hom_C(L−,−).

It remains to compare the action on morphisms. Let (u,v):(A,X) → (A′,X′) be a morphism in D^op × C. Thus v:X → X′ is a morphism in C, and u:A → A′ in D^op corresponds to a morphism ū:A′ → A in D. The arrow L^op(u):LA → LA′ in C^op corresponds to L(ū):LA′ → LA in C. By the definition of the ordinary hom bifunctor, its action on the pair (L^op(u),v) sends an element h:LA → X to

v ∘ h ∘ L(ū):LA′ → X′.

On the other hand, by definition, the hom bifunctor with left functor Hom_C(L−,−) acts on (u,v) by exactly the same rule: h ↦ v ∘ h ∘ L(ū). Hence the two functors have the same value on every object and the same map on every morphism. Consequently,

Hom_C(L−,−) = Hom_C(−,−) ∘ (L^op × id_C).

Thus the intended claim holds after correcting the two displayed domain/codomain errors noted above.
